title: The d- and f-Block Elements

standard_text: General introduction, electronic configuration, occurrence and characteristics of transition metals, general trends in properties of the first row transition metals – metallic character, ionization enthalpy, oxidation states, ionic radii, colour, catalytic property, magnetic properties, interstitial compounds, alloy formation. key_sub: Partly filled d orbitals give colour, paramagnetism and catalysis.
body_html:
How to think about it

Transition metals have partly filled d orbitals in their atoms or common ions; Zn, Cd and Hg (d¹⁰) are not typical transition elements. Because the (n − 1)d and ns energies are close, they show variable oxidation states. Unpaired d electrons make compounds coloured (d–d transitions) and paramagnetic, with μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM.

Potassium permanganate and dichromate are strong oxidising agents in acid. The lanthanoids (4f) show +3 states and a steady fall in size, the lanthanoid contraction; the actinoids (5f) are radioactive and show more oxidation states.

Example

Fe²⁺ (3d⁶). Unpaired electrons?

high spin

Answer: 4

Example

μ for 3 unpaired electrons?

√15

Answer: 3.87 BM

Common mistakes

  • Counting 4s electrons in the ion.
  • Calling Zn a transition metal.
  • Using √n instead of √(n(n + 2)).

faq.q: Why are many transition metal compounds coloured?
faq.a: Their partly filled d orbitals allow d–d transitions that absorb visible light.
The gradual decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series because 4f electrons shield poorly.
